Welcome to my portfolio for MUSA 5080: Public Policy Analytics at the University of Pennsylvania.
This site documents my work in the Master of Urban Spatial Analytics program — weekly notes, course assignments, and a final project applying data analysis to urban policy questions.







Selfie while climbing in the Palisades, CA


Hi! I’m currently a graduate student in the MUSA program at UPenn. I come from a computer science background, but with a lifelong passion for cartography and data visualization that’s led me to this program. Most of my previous research has dealt with environmental remote sensing, machine learning, and computer vision.

filter() -> picks rows # filteR has an R in it!
select() -> picks columns # seleCt has a C in it!
mutate() -> add a new computed column

Example: new <- mutate(counties, income2)

arrange() -> change order of rows
group_by() -> similar to SQL GROUP BY; many rows become few

Collapses similar rows into one group

summarize() -> collapse data frame into one row of summary statistics









Tip



Step1 <- filter(counties, moe_PCT > 10)
Step2 <- arrange(Step1, desc(moe_PCT))
Step3 <- Select(NAME, moe_PCT) # create dataFrame


This works, but it leads to messy files and excess code.


%>% -> chains together operations in R






Tip



New_data <- Counties %>%
filter(moe_PCT) %>%
arrange(desc(moe_PCT))%>%
Select(NAME, moe_PCT)







The best source of data on the US population; started by James Madison.
Decennial Census

Every 10 years, exactly 10 questions are asked of every person that is in the US
Basic questions on household size, age, etc.

American Community Survey (ACS)

Started in 2005
Sample of the population gets more interesting questions such as “do you drive a car to work” or “what’s your annual income?”
Approximately 3 percent of households are surveyed
From that sample, we come up with an estimate for the entire population
2 versions: 1 year (for places >65,000 people), and a 5-year running average (block group tract)

Example:
B19013-001E
B -> base table
901 -> table number
00 -> line number
E -> estimate
M -> MOE (margin of error)
library(tidycensus)
load_variables()

State->County->Tract (boundaries change all the time!)
GEOID
421010001001 (11 digits)

42 (first 2): state
101 (next 3): county
0001001 (last ones): tract







Tip



data <- get_acs(geography = “county”, variables = c(“B19013_001”,“B01003_001”), state = “PA”, year = 2023, survey = “acs5”)


When running this code, we get the data in TIDY(long) format. We can add output = “wide” to display in TIDY(wide) format.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
In this analysis, I’m looking to see how population and the measurement of reliability are related, using the number of college-educated individuals in each county as an example.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Pulling the data

my_state <- "CA"        # two-letter abbreviation of state
my_variable <- "B15003_022"     # variable code


county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

This code displays the first few rows of our new county_data table.

dim(county_data)

[1] 58  5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                         variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                        <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 06001 Alameda County, California   B15003_022   341463  4001
2 06003 Alpine County, California    B15003_022      264   102
3 06005 Amador County, California    B15003_022     5027   492
4 06007 Butte County, California     B15003_022    28185  1349
5 06009 Calaveras County, California B15003_022     5242   616
6 06011 Colusa County, California    B15003_022     1579   339








Tip



Each of the 58 counties in CA are represented in this table, with GEOID, name of the county, variable name, estimate, and margin of error forming the 5 columns.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)


county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                         estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                           <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Sierra County, California         325   130    40  
 2 Alpine County, California         264   102    38.6
 3 Trinity County, California       1164   309    26.5
 4 Modoc County, California         1031   234    22.7
 5 Colusa County, California        1579   339    21.5
 6 Mono County, California          1814   370    20.4
 7 Del Norte County, California     2540   432    17.0
 8 Glenn County, California         2314   379    16.4
 9 Mariposa County, California      2582   401    15.5
10 Plumas County, California        2031   313    15.4


Sierra County and Alpine County have by far the greatest MOE, followed by Trinity, Modoc, and Colusa Counties.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    28
2 Low confidence     17
3 Moderate           13


Using our reliability cutoffs, 28 counties fall into a “high confidence” category, 13 into “moderate confidence”, and 17 into “low confidence”. The percentiles were chosen somewhat arbitrarily, but they seem reasonable for this assignment.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 06001 Alameda County, California   341463   4001 1651949    NA
2 06003 Alpine County, California       264    102    1695   234
3 06005 Amador County, California      5027    492   41029    NA
4 06007 Butte County, California      28185   1349  209470    NA
5 06009 Calaveras County, California   5242    616   45995    NA
6 06011 Colusa County, California      1579    339   21895    NA


In this table, popE = estimate, and popM = MOE.

county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

The following block compares the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         28       1310938.
2 Low confidence          10         15660.
3 Moderate                20        118996.


We can see here that population is clearly correlated with confidence in deriving the population statistics; high-confidence counties have by far the highest population, and low-confidence counties have by far the lowest population numbers.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
Sierra County, located in a rural area in Northern California, has the state’s second-lowest population and scored the lowest in our reliability estimate. The neighboring Alpine County, which has the lowest population in the state, only scored slightly higher. Conversely, Los Angeles County, which has the highest population in the state, had the highest score for reliability.
This trend is related to how the ACS collects data; since it is based on a sample percentage rather than a complete survey of every person in the county, smaller counties have less people included in the study. With a smaller sample size, chances are higher that there may be variations in the study that aren’t necessarily representative of the whole. On the other hand, larger counties have larger samples that lead to more reliable estimates, as any variation is generally smoothed out the large number of observations.
For our variable (people with college educations), this could have the potential impact of improper funding allocation to areas that already have enough, as well as the diversion of education funds that could be sorely needed in a smaller county. For example, if it is improperly estimated that very people in Alpine County are college-educated (which is highly correlated with their children not going to college), while many people actually do want to go to college, the county could be passed over when it’s time to build a new university (like a CSU).

title: Week 3: Dplyr and more MOEs
text:
Key Concepts

Building Visualizations w/ GGPlot
Anscombe’s Quartet: four graphs with vastly different layouts have the same mean, correlation, and regression. This is why we need to analyze the graph, too!







Tip



A plot is a mapping from columns in your data to visual properties on your page. GG = “grammar of graphics”.




Using GGPlot
P <- ggplot(data) # this creates a blank canvas
aes(…) # aesthetic mappings; not decoration, only tell factual information on where the columns will go on the plot
geom() # the shape/type of chart






Tip



ggplot(tract_data) + aes(x=population, y=moe_pct) + geom_point(color=blue)





Inside aes()
Not inside aes()




aes(Color = reliability)
color = “example_color”



decorations





Geometry Options



What I want to know
GEOM




How a variable is spread
geom_histogram()


How 2 variables relate
geom_point()


How 2 variables compare
geom_boxplot() or geom(col)


How things change over time
geom_line()


How uncertain is a value
geom_errorbar()





Error Bar Charts






Tip



county_data %>% ggplot(aes(x = NAME, y = estimate))
+ geom_col()
+ geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe))


This plot is extremely messy, and I’ll get killed if I turn that in.

This is a better version that cleans up some of the issues.






Tipreduce to 15 most unreliable.



county_data %>% arrange(desc(moe_pct))
%>% slice_head(n = 15)
%>% ggplot(aes(x = NAME, y = estimate))
+ geom_col()
+ geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe))

Flip to make names more readable:
county_data %>% arrange(desc(moe_pct))
%>% slice_head(n = 15)
%>% ggplot(aes(x = NAME, y = estimate))
+ geom_col()
+ geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe))
+ coord_flip()


Sort bars by bar length rather than alphabetically:
county_data %>% arrange(desc(moe_pct))
%>% slice_head(n = 15)
%>% ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate))
+ geom_col()
+ geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe))
+ coord_flip()


Remove “County, New York”
county_data %>% arrange(desc(moe_pct))
%>% mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, ” County, New York”))
%>% slice_head(n = 15) %>% ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate))
+ geom_col()
+ geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe))
+ coord_flip()


Change to narrower width of the error bars
county_data %>% arrange(desc(moe_pct))
%>% mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, ” County, New York”))
%>% slice_head(n = 15) %>% ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate))
+ geom_col()
+ geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe), width = 0.3)
+ coord_flip()


Tidy up with a nice theme:
county_data %>% arrange(desc(moe_pct))
%>% mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, ” County, New York”))
%>% slice_head(n = 15)
%>% ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate))
+ geom_col(fill = “steelblue”)
+ geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe), width = 0.3)
+ coord_flip()
+ theme_minimal()


Fix labels and numbers:
county_data %>% arrange(desc(moe_pct))
%>% mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, ” County, New York”))
%>% slice_head(n = 15)
%>% ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate)) + geom_col(fill = “steelblue”) +
geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe), width = 0.3) + coord_flip() +
theme_minimal() + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
labs( title = “Counties with the largest margins of error”, subtitle = “People below 100% of the poverty level, ACS 2023 5-year estimates”, x = NULL, y = “Population below poverty level” )






Coefficient of Variation (CV)
This is a relative measure of sampling error.
Low CV -> 15%; high reliability
Medium CV-> 15-30%; medium reliability
High CV -> 30+%; high sampling error, low reliability
moe_sum() -> adding estimates together
moe_prop -> one estimate as share of another
moe_ratio() -> poverty_num / household_income






Tip



90% of the time in a normal distribution, the value will fall within 1.645 standard deviations of the mean.




ACS MOE

Tells us the 90% confidence interval; a higher value is worse
Estimate could be 20% +- 3.0 standard deviations

title: Week 4: Spatial Joins and GIS with R
text:
GIS with R

Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)

2 main families of CRS: geographic and projected

Geographic Coordinate System (datum): units are in degrees from center of Earth

Ellipsoid used to approximate the geoid; many different kinds of ellipsoids with different flattening ratios
NAD27 -> first datum/geographic coordinate system
WGS84 is GPS standard
Line of latitude is at equator; line of longitude is at the Prime Meridian
Lat is flat

Projected Coordinate System: need to flatten geoid into a 2D surface

Conic, cylindrical, and planar coordinate systems
Projections can either preserve shapes, areas, distance, or direction

Make sure you’re checking if your state plane is in feet or meters
If state plane isn’t convenient (for long/large states), use UTM zones



All spatial data comes with a coordinate reference system; it comes with a geometry column that has coordinates






Tip



st_set_crs() -> 2272 # adds the correct CRS label, but doesn’t change actual coordinates
st_transform(data, 2272) # actually changes coordinate system
